title: Episode 4: The Learning Room
description: Your shared practice environment: challenges, PR workflow, bot feedback, peer review.
concepts: What the Learning Room repository is and its purpose
The fork-edit-PR workflow for submitting solutions
How the automated bot provides feedback on your pull request
Peer review: reading and commenting on classmate work
Why low-stakes practice builds real confidence
How to find your challenge and know when you are done
transcriptText:
﻿[ALEX]
Welcome back. Today we're getting oriented to something you'll use constantly in the workshop: your Learning Room. Think of it as your personal practice repository on GitHub, built so you can learn the full workflow safely and realistically.

[JAMIE]
So this is not just a folder somewhere. It's an actual GitHub repository with issues, branches, pull requests, and automation?

[ALEX]
Exactly. When you accept the GitHub Classroom assignment, GitHub makes a private copy of the workshop template repository for you. That copy lives in the workshop organization and is named something like learning-room-your-username. You get write access to that repo. You can create branches there, open pull requests there, and receive automated feedback there.

[JAMIE]
And just to clear up a very common beginner question: am I supposed to work in the original template repository?

[ALEX]
No. You do not work directly in the shared template. The template is the clean source maintained by facilitators. Your work happens only in your own private Learning Room repository.

[JAMIE]
So each student gets a separate copy that starts with the same files, but our work stays separate.

[ALEX]
Right. You won't see other students' work inside your repo, and they won't see yours by default. That separation is intentional. It gives you a safe place to practice. It also means you do not need to create your own GitHub organization or change repository permissions. The facilitators handle the organization, the Classroom setup, the template, and the automation permissions.

[PAUSE]

[JAMIE]
Why go to the trouble of giving every student a separate repo instead of putting everyone in one shared practice repository?

[ALEX]
Three big reasons: safety, authenticity, and pace. Safety means you can experiment, make mistakes, and recover without affecting anyone else. Authenticity means you still practice real GitHub work: issues, branches, pull requests, reviews, checks, and merges. And pace means you can move through the Day 1 challenges at the speed that works for you. You're not blocking other students, and they aren't blocking you.

[JAMIE]
So it's private and low risk, but still close to real open source work.

[ALEX]
That's the idea. Later you'll contribute in a more public, shared setting. The Learning Room is where you build muscle memory first: issue, branch, pull request, review, merge.

[PAUSE]

[JAMIE]
Let's walk through getting into it, because I know this first setup moment can feel stressful.

[ALEX]
Absolutely. The starting point is the Day 1 GitHub Classroom assignment link. Before you begin, make sure you're signed into your GitHub account in your browser. You'll also need the assignment link from the facilitator. It usually looks like classroom dot github dot com slash a slash some random ID.

[JAMIE]
What happens when I open that link?

[ALEX]
You'll land on a page hosted on classroom dot github dot com. Your screen reader should announce a heading with the assignment name, something like the workshop title and Day 1. If GitHub Classroom asks for authorization to access your GitHub account, activate the Authorize GitHub Classroom button. That's usually a one-time step.

[JAMIE]
And sometimes it asks you to identify yourself from a roster, right?

[ALEX]
Yes. If that page appears, use arrow keys through the list, or use Find in Page with Control F or Command F to search for your name. Activate the control next to your name. If you can't find your name, choose the link to skip to the next step, then tell the facilitator in chat so they can reconcile the roster afterward.

[JAMIE]
Then comes the actual accept button.

[ALEX]
Right. Activate Accept this assignment, or Accept the assignment. After that, you'll get a status page. It may say something like, You are ready to go. Behind the scenes, GitHub Classroom is copying the learning-room-template repository into the workshop organization and granting you access. That usually takes about ten to thirty seconds.

[JAMIE]
And this is one of those places where a screen reader user may need a little extra patience.

[ALEX]
Definitely. The page may not automatically announce when your repository is ready. Refresh the page every fifteen seconds or so, or use browse mode and press K to move through links until you hear a link to your new repository. The repository URL will look like github dot com slash workshop-org slash learning-room-your-username.

[JAMIE]
Once I open that repository, what should I confirm?

[ALEX]
Three things. First, the repository name matches learning-room-your-username. Second, the About area or repository description confirms it's your private workshop copy. Third, you can see folders and files that came from the template, such as docs, dot github, and README dot md. And bookmark this page, because you'll return to it repeatedly.

[PAUSE]

[JAMIE]
What about the first challenge?

[ALEX]
When your Learning Room is ready, Challenge 1 should appear as an issue in your repository. Facilitators prepare that through the progression bot. From the repository page, go to the Issues tab. If you know GitHub keyboard shortcuts, G then I opens Issues. Look for an open issue with a title like Challenge 1: Find Your Way Around, often authored by a bot account like aria-bot or github-actions bot.

[JAMIE]
And the issue body tells you what to do next.

[ALEX]
Exactly. It explains the task, where to find evidence, and how to submit your completion.

[JAMIE]
What if Challenge 1 doesn't show up?

[ALEX]
If it's still missing after about two minutes, refresh the Issues tab once. If it's still not there, open the Actions tab and check whether the Student Progression Bot workflow ran successfully. If it failed or never ran, send the facilitator the link to your repository in workshop chat. They can trigger the student-progression workflow or create Challenge 1 from the issue template.

[JAMIE]
And before we leave setup, we also want to confirm Gandalf exists.

[ALEX]
Yes. Gandalf is the pull request validation bot. Open the Actions tab and look for a workflow named pr-validation-bot or Gandalf PR Validation. You don't need to run it yet. You just want to confirm the workflow is present so you know automated PR feedback is wired up.

[PAUSE]

[JAMIE]
So by the end of this first setup sequence, I should have my own private repo, at least one challenge issue, and visible automation workflows.

[ALEX]
That's a great summary. And this part of the curriculum is really orientation. There are no challenges in this chapter itself, and no automation check tied directly to it. It's here to prepare you for the issue-based challenges that begin next.

[JAMIE]
Is there a readiness check before moving on?

[ALEX]
Yes. Before starting the challenge chapters, you should be able to do three things: find docs slash CHALLENGES dot md in your Learning Room repository, explain the flow issue to branch to pull request to review to merge, and identify where Gandalf's bot feedback appears on a pull request, which is the Conversation tab.

[PAUSE]

[JAMIE]
Now let's talk about the two-track idea, because this can be confusing. There are the GitHub Skills modules, and then there's the Learning Room.

[ALEX]
Right. These are two separate but reinforcing tracks, both using your own GitHub account. Track one is the GitHub Skills modules. Those are optional and self-paced. Examples include Introduction to GitHub, Communicate Using Markdown, and Review Pull Requests.

[JAMIE]
Those are the ones where GitHub's learning bot walks you through steps?

[ALEX]
Yes. In that track, the automated guide is Mona. The purpose there is focused skill practice: creating a branch, opening a pull request, merging, writing markdown, reviewing pull requests, and similar basics.

[JAMIE]
And the second track is the required workshop track in the Learning Room.

[ALEX]
Exactly. That's where the workshop's Day 1 challenge sequence lives. Early blocks focus on things like finding your way around the repository, filing issues, branching, committing, opening a pull request, and even handling a merge conflict. Later blocks move into collaboration culture, merging, and community tools like labels, milestones, and notifications.

[JAMIE]
So one track is optional skill drills, and the other is the required guided practice environment for the workshop.

[ALEX]
That's a clean way to say it. They complement each other, but they are not the same. One important learning card idea here is: two tracks, one account. You may use the same GitHub account for both, but the context, bots, and goals differ.

[JAMIE]
Can we compare them directly?

[ALEX]
Sure. Skills modules are public or personal learning exercises managed by GitHub's own teaching flow, usually in repositories created for those modules. The Learning Room is your private workshop repository in the classroom organization. Skills modules are optional. The Learning Room is required for the workshop. Mona guides the Skills modules; Gandalf and the progression system support the Learning Room. And the Learning Room is sequenced around workshop challenges, peer practice, and accessibility-focused open source contribution habits.

[PAUSE]

[JAMIE]
Let's get concrete about what's inside the repo. What's the folder structure for?

[ALEX]
At a high level, your Learning Room contains documentation files you'll edit, automation files under dot github, a README, and a challenge menu. The docs folder is especially important because that's where much of your practice work lives.

[JAMIE]
And before editing, we need a practice branch.

[ALEX]
Yes. This matters a lot. You create a separate branch so your work is isolated from the main branch. That protects the stable version of the repository and lets you package your changes in a pull request.

[JAMIE]
So the branch is like a safe workspace where I can try things before proposing them.

[ALEX]
Exactly. That's the reason for a separate branch: isolation, reviewability, and alignment with standard GitHub flow. You don't make challenge edits directly on main unless a specific exercise tells you to. Instead, create your branch, switch to it, make your changes there, and then open a pull request back into main.

[JAMIE]
How should learners think about using that branch day to day?

[ALEX]
Usually like this: read the issue, create a branch named for the task, switch to that branch, make and save your changes, commit them, push if you're working locally, and open a pull request. If you're editing directly on GitHub's website, GitHub often helps you create a branch as part of that edit flow.

[JAMIE]
And there's also a practical tool-card idea here: know how to switch to your practice branch.

[ALEX]
Right. In GitHub's web interface, branch switching often happens through the branch selector near the top of the file list. In VS Code or the command line, you switch branches with the tools available there. The essential concept is not memorizing every interface immediately. It's knowing what branch you're on before you start editing.

[PAUSE]

[JAMIE]
Let's tour the practice files, because these are the materials students actually work on.

[ALEX]
One important file is docs slash welcome dot md. This introduces open source contribution. It includes specific TODO sections learners complete.

[JAMIE]
What are those TODOs about?

[ALEX]
TODO 1 is the section called Who Can Contribute? The key idea is that open source contribution is not limited to expert programmers. People contribute through code, documentation, testing, design, accessibility feedback, issue triage, reproduction steps, community support, and more.

[JAMIE]
That's especially important in accessibility work, where lived experience and careful observation are genuine expertise.

[ALEX]
Absolutely. TODO 2 is about Finding Something to Work On. Learners should understand that contributors often start by reading project documentation, looking for labeled issues, exploring beginner-friendly tasks, checking contribution guides, and noticing gaps in clarity or accessibility. In other words, useful work is often discoverable if you know where to look.

[JAMIE]
And TODO 3?

[ALEX]
After Your Contribution Is Merged. That section helps learners see merging not as the end of participation, but as one step in an ongoing relationship with a project. After a contribution is merged, you might verify the change, thank reviewers, continue following the repository, help with future issues, or make another contribution.

[JAMIE]
So even that file is doing double duty: teaching content and giving practice with editing.

[ALEX]
Exactly. Another practice file is docs slash keyboard-shortcuts dot md, which serves as a screen reader shortcut reference. That's especially relevant for learners who need efficient keyboard-based navigation in GitHub, browser content, and related tools.

[JAMIE]
And there's also docs slash setup-guide dot md.

[ALEX]
Yes. That file is about getting ready to contribute. It reinforces preparation habits: making sure your tools are ready, understanding the repository workflow, and knowing what you need before participating in a contribution process.

[JAMIE]
Then docs slash CHALLENGES dot md is basically the menu of what's available.

[ALEX]
Right. It's the challenge menu for your Learning Room. Even though challenges may unlock progressively through issues, that file helps you understand the landscape of the exercises.

[JAMIE]
And there are bonus challenges too.

[ALEX]
Yes. Bonus challenges extend practice beyond the required path. They're useful if you finish early, want extra repetition, or want to stretch into more realistic contribution scenarios.

[PAUSE]

[JAMIE]
Now let's talk about pull request sharing, because this is where learners often wonder, Wait, if my repo is private and personal, how do review and collaboration happen?

[ALEX]
Great question. The Learning Room is private by default, but collaboration is still practiced through a structured flow. Here's the general sequence.

[JAMIE]
Step one: the student opens a pull request.

[ALEX]
Yes. Imagine Student A is working on Challenge 3, completing the welcome guide. They create or update a branch, make the required edits, and open a pull request from that branch into main in their own repository. That pull request becomes the place where changes, comments, and checks come together.

[JAMIE]
Then automation validates it.

[ALEX]
Correct. A workflow such as dot github slash workflows slash learning-room-pr-bot dot yml can run validation. Gandalf or a related automation reviews whether the pull request appears to meet the exercise expectations and posts educational feedback.

[JAMIE]
Not just pass or fail, but teaching feedback.

[ALEX]
Exactly. In a learning environment, the bot is there to coach, not just gatekeep.

[JAMIE]
Then comes peer review, but facilitator-arranged.

[ALEX]
Right. Because repositories are private, peer review access is intentionally arranged. Visibility is controlled. Facilitators may pair students and grant the needed access so one learner can review another learner's pull request.

[JAMIE]
So this is not a free-for-all where everyone sees everything.

[ALEX]
No. Access is managed. Next, the reviewer reads and comments. If you're the assigned reviewer, you open the paired student's pull request, read the changed files, and leave comments or an overall review. Again, visibility is limited to those who were intentionally given access.

[JAMIE]
Then the author responds and updates.

[ALEX]
Yes. If you're the pull request author, you read the feedback, decide what revisions to make, update your branch, and let the pull request reflect those new commits. That response process is part of the learning. And once more, visibility is controlled within the arrangement set by facilitators.

[JAMIE]
And then we get to merge and celebration.

[ALEX]
Exactly. When the review is approved, or when the workflow for that exercise allows self-merge, the author merges the pull request. After merge, a progression bot can post the next challenge issue. That's how the learning path advances one step at a time. The visibility of all of this remains scoped to the people who need access.

[JAMIE]
So one learning card idea here is that pull request sharing is structured, intentional, and supported by both bots and people.

[ALEX]
Well said.

[PAUSE]

[JAMIE]
Let's make the visibility piece really explicit. What do you see, and what do your peers see?

[ALEX]
By default, you see your own repository contents: your issues, your branches, your pull requests, your checks, and your bot feedback. Other students do not automatically see your work. Peer visibility happens only when facilitators intentionally pair or grant access for a review activity. That's a key privacy and learning design feature.

[JAMIE]
So if someone is nervous about making mistakes in front of the whole class, this setup reduces that pressure.

[ALEX]
Exactly. You still practice authentic review, but without unnecessary exposure.

[PAUSE]

[JAMIE]
Can we break down the learning automation system itself?

[ALEX]
Yes. There are three main kinds of feedback timing in this environment. Type 1 is automated bot feedback, often within about thirty seconds. That's the fast response you may see after opening or updating a pull request. It checks structure, expected edits, or workflow conditions.

[JAMIE]
Type 2 is peer reviewer feedback.

[ALEX]
Right. That usually takes longer, maybe fifteen to sixty minutes depending on workshop timing and pairing. This is human feedback: interpretation, encouragement, suggestions, and questions.

[JAMIE]
And Type 3?

[ALEX]
Progress tracking on merge. When a pull request is merged, the system can update your progression by posting the next challenge or marking your advancement. That creates a clear sense that merging isn't just administrative. It actually moves your workshop journey forward.

[PAUSE]

[JAMIE]
What about study groups?

[ALEX]
Study groups are optional. Learners may discuss concepts, compare notes, or work alongside each other while still making their own repository changes. For example, two students might read the same challenge together over a call, talk through what a pull request is, and then each complete the task separately in their own Learning Room.

[JAMIE]
So collaboration in understanding is welcome, even when repository work remains individual.

[ALEX]
Exactly.

[PAUSE]

[JAMIE]
Let's revisit the key differences between a Skills module and the Learning Room, because that's likely to appear on learners' mental quiz later.

[ALEX]
Here are the essentials. Skills modules are optional, self-paced, and guided by GitHub's bot, Mona. The Learning Room is required for the workshop, lives in the workshop organization, and is private to you unless access is intentionally shared. Skills modules focus on isolated skills. The Learning Room ties those skills into a coherent contribution workflow with issues, branching, pull requests, review, merge, and progression through workshop challenges.

[JAMIE]
So if I'm wondering, Which one counts for the workshop? The answer is the Learning Room.

[ALEX]
Correct.

[PAUSE]

[JAMIE]
Now let's help learners review a peer's pull request well, because many people are more nervous about reviewing than authoring.

[ALEX]
That's common. First, finding pull requests to review usually happens through facilitator pairing or explicit assignment, not random browsing. If you are assigned a review, you'll receive the repository and pull request link you need.

[JAMIE]
Once I'm in the assigned pull request, how should I read it?

[ALEX]
Start with the pull request title and description so you know the goal. Then inspect the changed files. Compare what's in the pull request against the challenge instructions. Ask: Did the author address the requested sections? Is the writing clear? Did they preserve formatting? Are there accessibility or clarity improvements to suggest?

[JAMIE]
And when leaving a review?

[ALEX]
Be specific, respectful, and actionable. Point to exact lines when possible. Distinguish between required changes and optional suggestions. If something works well, say that too. Good review is not just error detection; it's communication.

[JAMIE]
What about responding to feedback as the author?

[ALEX]
Read comments carefully. If the suggestion makes sense, update your branch and reply briefly so the reviewer knows what changed. If you're confused, ask a clarifying question. If you disagree, respond respectfully and explain your reasoning. The learning card here is that pull request sharing is a conversation, not a verdict.

[PAUSE]

[JAMIE]
Let's do the FAQ lightning round.

[ALEX]
Let's do it.

[JAMIE]
Can I see other students' pull requests?

[ALEX]
Not by default. Repositories are private, and access is intentionally limited unless facilitators pair you for review.

[JAMIE]
What if I don't agree with my assigned reviewer?

[ALEX]
Start by asking clarifying questions and explaining your reasoning respectfully. If needed, involve a facilitator. Disagreement can be part of healthy review, especially when handled thoughtfully.

[JAMIE]
Will my pull request get lost when everyone is working at once?

[ALEX]
In this setup, no. Your work is in your own repository, and progression is tracked there. The whole design reduces the chaos of one giant shared queue.

[JAMIE]
Can I comment on someone else's pull request?

[ALEX]
Only if you've been given access, such as through an assigned review pairing.

[JAMIE]
What if my reviewer doesn't respond?

[ALEX]
Wait a reasonable amount of time, then contact the facilitator. Remember that peer feedback may take fifteen to sixty minutes depending on workshop flow.

[JAMIE]
Can I work with a friend?

[ALEX]
Yes, in the sense of discussing ideas or studying together, especially in optional study groups. But each learner should complete their own repository work unless the exercise explicitly says otherwise.

[JAMIE]
How long does review take?

[ALEX]
Bot feedback is usually fast, around thirty seconds. Human review varies more, often fifteen to sixty minutes.

[JAMIE]
What if bot feedback is wrong?

[ALEX]
Treat the bot as helpful automation, not infallible authority. Recheck the instructions, inspect your pull request, and ask a facilitator if the bot seems mistaken.

[JAMIE]
Do I need to complete every challenge?

[ALEX]
Follow the workshop requirements for required challenges first. Bonus challenges are extra. If you're unsure what is expected, check the challenge menu or ask the facilitators.

[PAUSE]

[JAMIE]
If a learner gets stuck anywhere in this process, what's the best advice?

[ALEX]
Pause and locate where the process broke. Is it account access, Classroom acceptance, finding the repo, missing issues, branch confusion, or pull request feedback? Then use the available support: reread the issue, check the Actions tab, inspect the Conversation tab on the pull request, consult the challenge menu, ask your study group if you're using one, and message the facilitator in chat when needed. Getting stuck is normal in GitHub workflows. The important skill is learning how to diagnose the stuck point.

[JAMIE]
That's reassuring, especially for learners who may be balancing a screen reader, browser navigation, new terminology, and GitHub's interface all at once.

[ALEX]
Exactly. Friction is not failure. It's part of learning a real tool.

[PAUSE]

[JAMIE]
I also want to pause on the emotional message of this chapter. The repository is called the Learning Room for a reason.

[ALEX]
Yes. This is a place to practice contribution, not a test you must perform perfectly in public. By opening issues, creating branches, editing files, opening pull requests, receiving feedback, and merging, you are already doing the work of contributing. That matters.

[JAMIE]
So even before the larger open source project work, this counts as real contribution practice.

[ALEX]
It does. You're learning the habits and structures that make open source collaboration possible.

[PAUSE]

[JAMIE]
Before we close, can you mention the trusted references behind this material?

[ALEX]
Yes. The chapter points learners toward authoritative GitHub documentation, including topics like README files, editing files, GitHub flow, pull requests, and general Git and GitHub docs. Those references are useful when you want the official platform explanation alongside the workshop guidance.

[JAMIE]
So the workshop gives the learning path, and the official docs provide deeper confirmation and detail.

[ALEX]
Exactly. Put together, they make a strong support system.

[JAMIE]
All right. So your next move is simple: make sure your Learning Room exists, confirm Challenge 1 is there, know where docs slash CHALLENGES dot md lives, and be ready to move through the flow from issue to branch to pull request to review to merge.

[ALEX]
And remember: your Learning Room is private, personal, and purposeful. It's your place to build confidence before contributing in bigger shared spaces.

[PAUSE]

# The Learning Room: Your Personal Practice Repository
>
> **Listen to Episode 4:** [The Learning Room](https://lp.csedesigns.com/ggg/PODCASTS.html) - a conversational audio overview of this chapter. Listen before reading to preview the concepts, or after to reinforce what you learned.

> **Related appendices:** [Appendix A: Glossary](appendix-a-glossary.md) | [Appendix C: Markdown Reference](appendix-c-markdown-reference.md)
> **Authoritative sources:** [GitHub Docs: About README files](https://docs.github.com/en/repositories/managing-your-repositorys-settings-and-features/customizing-your-repository/about-readmes) | [GitHub Docs: Editing files](https://docs.github.com/en/repositories/working-with-files/managing-files/editing-files)

## What Is the Learning Room?

The **Learning Room** is your **own private GitHub repository** for the workshop. When you accept the GitHub Classroom assignment in Block 0, GitHub copies the [`Community-Access/learning-room-template`](https://github.com/Community-Access/learning-room-template) repository into the workshop classroom organization as `<workshop-org>/learning-room-<your-username>`. That copy is yours to use for the workshop - you have write access, your own branches, your own pull requests, and your own automated feedback from Gandalf the PR validation bot.

You do **not** work directly in `Community-Access/learning-room-template`. Think of the template as the clean master copy facilitators maintain. Your work happens in the private Learning Room repository created for you by GitHub Classroom.

Throughout this chapter and the rest of Day 1, "your Learning Room repository" or "your Learning Room repo" refers to this private copy. Every student gets one, and every copy starts from the same template files. You will not see other students' work in your repo, and they will not see yours - but everyone is doing the same challenges in parallel. Peer-simulation issues and pull requests inside your repo provide realistic collaboration practice, and facilitators may also pair students for real peer review when access is intentionally provided.

You do **not** need to create a GitHub organization or change repository permission settings. The workshop organization, template repository, Classroom assignment, and GitHub Actions permissions are managed by the facilitators.

## Why a Per-Student Repo?

GitHub Classroom gives each participant their own repository for three reasons:

- **Safety** -- you can experiment, break things, and recover without affecting anyone else
- **Authenticity** -- you practice real repository work: issues, branches, pull requests, checks, reviews, and merging
- **Pace** -- you progress through the 9 Day 1 challenges as fast or as slow as you need; nobody is waiting on you and you are not blocking anybody else

Real open source projects are shared spaces, and you will absolutely contribute to one on Day 2 (`accessibility-agents`) and through the Bonus C challenge. The Learning Room exists so you can build the muscle memory for issue, branch, PR, review, merge in a space where every mistake is a learning opportunity, not a public problem.

## Step-by-Step: Accept Your Classroom Assignment and Open Your Repo

This is the very first hands-on step of Day 1. By the end of this walkthrough you will have your own Learning Room repository on GitHub and your first challenge issue waiting for you. The whole flow takes about five minutes.

> **What you need before you start:**
>
> - A GitHub account you are signed into in your browser ([Pre-Workshop Setup, Step 1](00-pre-workshop-setup.md#step-1---create-your-github-account))
> - The **Classroom assignment link** -- the facilitator pastes this link in the workshop chat at the start of Block 0. It looks like `https://classroom.github.com/a/<random-id>`. If you do not have it, ask in chat or DM the facilitator.

### 1. Open the assignment link

1. In the same browser where you are signed into GitHub, open the Classroom assignment link the facilitator shared.
2. The page that loads is hosted on `classroom.github.com`. Your screen reader announces a heading with the assignment name (for example, "Git Going with GitHub").
3. If the page asks you to authorize **GitHub Classroom** to access your GitHub account, activate **Authorize GitHub Classroom**. This is a one-time step.

### 2. Identify yourself (if asked)

GitHub Classroom may ask you to pick your name from a roster so the facilitators can match your GitHub username to the registration list.

1. If a roster page appears, navigate the list with arrow keys or use Find-in-Page (`Ctrl+F` / `Cmd+F`) to search for your name.
2. Activate the link or button next to your name.
3. If you do not see your name on the roster, activate the **Skip to the next step** link and tell the facilitator in chat. They will reconcile the roster after your repo is created.

### 3. Accept the assignment

1. You now see a screen with a button that says **Accept this assignment** (or just **Accept the assignment**). Activate it.
2. The page changes to a status screen that says something like "You are ready to go!" with a refresh option. GitHub Classroom is now copying the `learning-room-template` repository into the workshop classroom organization and granting you access to your private copy. This usually takes 10-30 seconds.
3. Activate the **Refresh** link (or reload the page with `F5`) every 15 seconds or so until you see a link to your new repository. The link looks like `https://github.com/<workshop-org>/learning-room-<your-username>`.

> **Screen reader tip:** The status page does not auto-announce when the repo is ready. Use Browse mode and press `K` to step through links until you hear your repository link, or refresh the page until it appears.

### 4. Open your new repository

1. Activate the link to your repository. You land on the standard GitHub repo page for `<workshop-org>/learning-room-<your-username>`.
2. Verify three things on this page:
   - The **repo name** in the heading matches `learning-room-<your-username>`.
   - The **About** sidebar (or repo description) confirms this is a private workshop copy.
   - You see folders like `docs/`, `.github/`, and files like `README.md`. These came from the template.
3. Bookmark this page. You will return here for every Day 1 challenge.

### 5. Find your first challenge issue

## FAQ: Pull Requests in Your Learning Room

### "Can I see other students' PRs?"

Not inside their Learning Room repos -- those are private to each student. **You can see other participants' work in two ways:**

- During Challenge 3 ("Join the Conversation") and Challenge 8 ("Culture"), the facilitators pair you with classmates and add you as a collaborator on each other's repos so you can review.
- During Day 2 (and the Bonus C challenge), everyone contributes to the public `accessibility-agents` repo, where every PR is visible to everyone.

### "What if I don't agree with my assigned reviewer?"

When the facilitators pair you for peer review, the pairing is a starting point, not a mandate. You can request additional reviewers manually. Click "Reviewers" -> select someone else, or ask the facilitators to pair you differently.

### "Will my PR get lost when everyone is working at once?"

No. Your repo is your own; you only see your own PRs. Gandalf's feedback is on your PR alone, and any peer reviewer is specifically assigned to you.

### "Can I comment on someone else's PR?"

When the facilitators pair you for review, yes -- you will be added as a collaborator and can comment, approve, and request changes on their PR. On the public `accessibility-agents` repo, anyone can comment on any open PR.

### "What if my reviewer doesn't respond?"

Mention them directly in a PR comment: "@name, any thoughts on the changes I pushed?" Or ask a facilitator to follow up.

### "Can I work with a friend?"

The facilitators arrange peer pairings, but if you know someone else in the cohort and you want to review each other's work, ask either Jeff or Michael to add you to each other's repos.

### "How long does review take?"

When pairings happen during a workshop block, typically 15-60 minutes. If a reviewer is slow, the facilitators can step in or assign someone else.

### "What if bot feedback is wrong?"

Comment on the PR explaining why. Gandalf is intentionally educational, not punitive -- if you disagree with a check, the facilitators can override it. Gandalf is not perfect, which is exactly why human review still matters.

### "Do I need to complete every challenge?"

No. The Learning Room has challenges for all skill levels. You can pick what interests you, complete at your pace, and continue after the workshop -- your repo stays yours.

|---|---|
| Cannot find your `learn/<username>` branch | If you have not created it yet, follow Challenge 4. If you created it but cannot see it, refresh the branch selector or run `git fetch origin` from a local clone. |
| Push rejected to main branch | Main is protected. You need to push to your `learn/<username>` branch: `git checkout learn/<your-username>` then push again. |
| I want to see another student's PR | Ask a facilitator -- when peer review is part of a challenge, they will add you as a collaborator on the other student's repo. |
| Practice file has no TODO markers | Verify you are on the correct branch. Run `git branch` to see your current branch. The main branch may have already been updated. |
